how: Members proposed a recognizable character or logo and began a parallel zergling, providing concrete work around which others could gather.
Calls invited members to build a shared mark, follow a current plan, and help defend threatened artwork.
A defense call received a bare commitment to help without a request for anything in return.
Site choice was constrained by a participant's judgment that the space was too small and would require many people to cover its background.
The defense post received a direct one-line acceptance, although the exchange cannot establish silent participation or the preference mechanism for every reader.
A proposal and its call for helpers can occupy the same post rather than forming two separately observable sequential stages.
Participants replaced a character proposal with a legible logo, sought representation of both game scenes, and proposed later accents and expansion.
Builders reported conflicting placement starts, checked a pixel against the mock-up, and described the logo taking shape.
A reference chart, pixel guide, and repeated coordinate sharing made collective placement actionable while participants asked strays to follow the design.
Calls and subsequent construction reports coexist with coordination failures, so the record supports mobilization followed by building without establishing that any particular call caused placement.
Publishing a template does not finally settle design when later changes require proposal, authorization, and incorporation into the common post.
This room occupies the model's decided-order minority through explicit design approval and diplomacy rules without contradicting the model's cross-room prevalence claim.
Recognized volunteer leads authorize a proposed design change before another organizer incorporates it into the public plan.
Incorporating a revised design into the common instructions depends on approval from recognized project leads.
Participants relay plans between chat and public coordination, returning logistics credits and coordinates while the backstage deliberation remains partly unseen.
A fairness objection to bot-made art establishes argument about automation but does not establish deployment or adjustment of machine placements by the project.
Manual cooldown participation and a bot-fairness objection do not reveal a transition from upkeep to deploying machines or prove that machines were unnecessary.
Members repair stray pixels, hand maintenance between regions, and rally defense of both the logo and the zergling.
Participants explicitly turn completion into maintenance because the standing design remains exposed to vandals and incoming projects.
Participants contest which neighbor caused damage, challenge an accuser's own pixel placement, and acknowledge accidental friendly damage.
Participants negotiate contested space, report chat agreements and turn-taking, and discuss whether the logo stays above or below another project's window.
Border talk begins during site selection before completion, making upkeep one trigger for negotiation rather than its necessary starting point.
Offers and requests for hosted space are visible, but the record does not establish uptake of the early offer or a host's continuing rule over the resulting work.
Members refuse to consume other projects, accept a small overlap, apologize for accidental damage, and instruct defenders to repair without retaliation.
A negotiated integration boundary supplies a grey stopping line that an organizer tries to enforce among placers.
Restraint can precede agreement as a reciprocal norm, while a settled boundary still leaves some placers pushing beyond it.
Participants exchange protection for border help, invite assistance with another build, and direct spare effort toward helpful neighbors.
Neighbor help is justified by deserved support and possible future reciprocity without an explicit claim that current upkeep has exhausted available hands.
A reported agreement explicitly exchanges leaving the zergling untouched for helping defend the partner's border.
A proposed alliance receives explicit acceptance and is described as protecting neighboring blue logos together.
The pact's stated protective purpose is supported, but reported alliance and survival do not establish that coalition participation caused the work to survive.
An ambassador presents an alliance proposal and receives directions to the project's recognized representatives.
Representative routing is visible, but recognized leads and approval rules do not establish that members disputed anyone's mandate to commit the group.
Agreements, recognized representatives, and imperfect border compliance do not show a transition into a dispute over who may bind the group.
Reported relocation can accommodate a recognized neighboring project rather than follow erasure, defeat, or a judgment of insufficient defenders.
Recognizing that disputed pixels belong to another community's project is given as the reason for moving away.
A site-capacity judgment and separately reported moves do not establish a capacity-driven relocation sequence for the same work.
Shared game identities and skill language frame recruitment and survival without requiring a preexisting rivalry to determine the canvas target.
Naming another fandom's symbol as a possible conversion target does not establish a quarrel carried into the canvas from before the event.
The conversion proposal supplies no stated historical tie or prior rivalry that explains why that target was selected.
Fake announcements invite play, hurt, skepticism, and checking, with a genuine result initially mistaken for an April Fools joke.
Play framing also hosts strategy, release troubleshooting, and reward checking for a playable joke rather than only uncertainty over whether a claim is real.
Participants ask to retain a temporary joke game mode for private fun, which preserves a noncanvas feature rather than continuing the canvas collective.
A returning contributor receives support for personal autonomy and an offer of credited proxy posting, a care practice not explained by canvas mobilization or bare acceptance.
A participant creates a megathread to contain repeated attack and alliance posts and preserve the subreddit's ordinary subject matter.
The megathread explicitly names repeated attack and alliance posts as its reason for centralizing canvas discussion.
Participants announce completion, celebrate survival, thank contributors and allies, and claim their own parts in the work.
A post announcing that the logo survived receives a direct collective celebration of completion.
Textual recollections mark shutdown, recount final repairs and damage, explain the event, and remember a restrained pixel conflict.
The survival announcement becomes a site for recollecting final repair and additional border damage, supporting textual remembrance rather than an inferred archival program.
Preferring to interpret an imperfect zergling pixel as a wink supports interpretive commemoration but does not establish contested editing of a shared canvas copy.
Celebration, mourning, and survival reports do not establish lasting reuse or organization, while retaining a separate joke game mode cannot evidence canvas continuation.
The visible record of the work's fate does not reveal a subsequent decision to carry the canvas effort into a durable project.
A member proposes converting another fandom's symbol, meeting the model's minimal attack-call range without proving a raid occurred or the room adopted it.
Recruitment precedes expansionary proposals, but the cited concepts do not establish that a call for builders caused members to turn toward attacking another work.
The creep proposal receives objections about overwriting other projects, retaliation risk, and the difference between the proposer's fun and harm to neighbors.
A visitor congratulates the room after a remembered pixel skirmish that is later described as brief and without harsh words.
Replies to the creep proposal show refusal and risk warnings rather than a resulting border deal, so this attack-to-negotiation transition remains unobserved.
The retrospective salute concerns a different encounter and cannot establish that the documented creep attack call generated continuing rivalry talk.
A second mark is already being built while the first mark's location remains undecided, allowing parallel starts rather than one room-wide construction sequence.
